chunks.title: A digital garden is a philosophy not a website
chunks.text:
TITLE: A digital garden is a philosophy not a website
TAGS: digitalgardens, pkm, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

A digital garden is more of a philosophy than a website. It's a mindset for how you approach work, in whatever craft you're in. It lowers the barrier to sharing something publicly while also holding you accountable to closing threads. As a neurodivergent, it's really helpful to let your brain go wherever it wants and follow what catches your eye. The danger is falling into paralysis: bookmarking, reading, consuming, and never creating. The garden fights that.

## Thought-based, not project-based

What makes it different from a blog or YouTube is that it's thought-based, not project-based. Thoughts are ephemeral. They bleed into each other. You can make connections across everything. There's no polished package to ship. You just put it out there and let it grow.

Mine lives at lukevz.com, with Bear as the private layer behind it. Hub: PKM MOC.

TAGS: ai, design, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

AI is an accelerator. It amplifies your existing process, it can't fix a bad one. If your way of solving problems is already solid, you should see an exponential return on efficiency and impact. If it's not, AI just makes that worse faster.

That's why I care so much about the fundamentals: Define the baseline first and the Six questions before touching any tools matter more with AI in the loop, not less. The flip side of this take is AI makes taste the differentiator. How much AI actually changes the core of design work versus the peripheral stuff, I hold loosely. I think the instinct and taste are irreplaceable, but I'm watching that one. More at Design MOC.

chunks.title: Define the baseline first
chunks.text:
TITLE: Define the baseline first
TAGS: design, opinions, processes
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

The first thing I do on any problem is define the baseline: what are people doing today? If users are working in a spreadsheet, I know what that experience feels like, and I know I should never deliver something worse than that.

Defining the baseline tells you what "better" actually means. If you skip it, you have no way to measure whether you succeeded. Most projects skip it and pay for it later. It pairs with the Six questions before touching any tools, which I run before opening any design tool. Both live in my broader take at Design MOC.

TAGS: designsystems, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

A design system isn't a component library. It's a shared language, and the components are just the output. The real work is the decisions behind them, the documentation, and getting people to actually adopt it.

That's the thing people get wrong most often, and it's why design systems are my specialty. I've spent most of my career building and managing them, including the PwC design system, and the pattern holds everywhere: a system succeeds or fails on adoption and shared understanding, not on how many components it ships. More on where this sits in my career at Design Systems MOC.

TITLE: My career runs from YouTube tutorials to Instinct
TAGS: careers, timelines
TYPE: log | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

I've been designing for about 12 to 13 years, depending on how you count. It started with YouTube tutorials and freelance work, went deep on UX and design systems at PwC, and landed at Instinct, where I design veterinary software today.

## The timeline

- 2012 to 2013: YouTube, self-started. Built a Mac OS app review and tutorial channel that grew to 30k+ subscribers and multi-million views. Taught myself writing, video, graphic design, and web from scratch.
- Around 2015 to 2018: Freelance. Solo client work in HTML/CSS, WordPress, graphic design, web design, and video production for local and regional businesses.
- 2018: Founded a creative production company, formalizing the freelance work into an official business.
- 2021: Blue Corona Inc, Senior Web Designer. Designed and built custom websites for 80+ home service companies. Fast-paced client work focused on marketing and delivery speed.
- 2022: PwC Digital, Products & Technology, Senior UX Designer. Led proof-of-concept product designs, pitched and rebuilt the company's design system in Figma, and drove a department-wide migration from Sketch, Abstract, and InVision to Figma, upskilling 120+ designers.
- 2023: PwC Digital, UX Manager / Design System Manager. Led and mentored a team of three designers, managed the design system servicing 3,000+ products globally, and was lead designer on SDLC Canvas, the firm's flagship AI product.
- End of 2025: Joined Instinct Science as Senior Product Designer.

Details on the big chapters: I pitched and led PwC's migration to Figma, I ran the design system serving 3000 products at PwC, SDLC Canvas was PwC's flagship AI product, and I design software for veterinarians at Instinct. Hub: Career MOC.

TAGS: design, opinions

Simple doesn't mean basic. Simple is the most elegant complexity: distilling something without sacrificing utility or value. That's the bar.

Getting there means iterating past the first workable answer, which is why I lean so hard on the Six questions before touching any tools up front. You can't distill a problem you haven't defined. Part of my core take at Design MOC.

chunks.file: areas/Six questions before touching any tools.md
chunks.title: Six questions before touching any tools
chunks.text:
TITLE: Six questions before touching any tools
TAGS: design, opinions, processes
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

Good design is an answer to a series of questions. Before anything else you need a crystal-clear understanding of the problem, and that's harder than it sounds. The more you try to define it, the more complex it feels. It's an uphill battle to figure out what the problem actually is, then to keep iterating until you can deliver the simplest version of a solution.

The six questions I always ask at the start:

- What problem are we solving?
- Who are we solving it for?
- Why are we solving it?
- Does it even need to be solved?
- Does it need to be solved now?
- Does it need to be solved by us?

I run these before touching any tools, right alongside Define the baseline first. The bar for the answer is Simple is the most elegant form of complexity. This is the core of my process at Design MOC.

chunks.file: areas/The best patterns come from the physical world not other apps.md
chunks.title: The best patterns come from the physical world not other apps
chunks.text:
TITLE: The best patterns come from the physical world not other apps
TAGS: design, opinions
TYPE: evergreen | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

Design is mostly systematic pattern recognition, but the patterns that matter most aren't from other software. They're from the physical world. How do people know to push versus pull a door? How do they know where to park? Those patterns feel completely natural because they've been adopted at mass scale, and the best digital UX borrows from them, not from what another app does.

## Copying apps is templating, not pattern recognition

A lot of designers copy other software thinking they're doing pattern recognition. They're not. They're templating. Real pattern recognition means finding what's already familiar and natural to people in everyday life, then adapting it.

The caveat: people are complex and different. Some metaphors land for some users and completely miss others. Constantly reusing digital heuristics that work in some contexts won't always translate. You have to stay attuned to why something feels natural, not just that it does. This is the belief I'd defend hardest at Design MOC, and it's the same instinct behind Simple is the most elegant form of complexity.

Designers need to think like business owners, not order-takers. Ask how someone got to the problem, not just how to solve the one they handed you.

It's the thing my 22-year-old self needed to hear: ask more questions about how people arrived at the problem, not just about the problem itself. It's easy to go hard on solving what someone puts in front of you. It's harder, and more valuable, to understand how they got there. It pairs with Do not get attached to your work, and the Six questions before touching any tools are how I put it into practice. More at Design MOC.

TITLE: 52 is about owning your thinking again
TAGS: projects, pkm, notes
TYPE: project | STATUS: growing
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17

52 is a local markdown-based note-taking app I'm building. The idea is to stop outsourcing your thinking to AI and get back to that feeling of being in control you get with pen and paper: just focused on taking good notes again, one work week at a time.

## How it works

The core is a notes surface where you capture meetings and ideas. Those can be turned into action items, which automatically get tracked on a tasks page. You can tag collaborators and stakeholders, then filter by person to pull up everything about them quickly. Achievements and milestones can be turned into "epochs" so you can zoom out from the week-to-week and see your actual impact over time. It's also essentially a live CV: you're building the record as you go instead of scrambling to reconstruct it when you need to make a career move.

The philosophy behind it is the same as AI makes taste the differentiator: never outsource your thinking. It sits alongside the digital garden in how I work in public. Hub: PKM MOC.

chunks.title: How I think about Design
chunks.text:
TITLE: How I think about Design
TAGS: design, synthesis
TYPE: synthesis | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17
SYNTHESIS across 14 notes

My design process is rooted in the belief that good design is an answer to a series of questions. Before touching any tools, I define the baseline to understand the current user experience and run through six fundamental questions to ensure we are solving the right problem for the right reasons. My goal is to achieve simplicity, which I define as the most elegant form of complexity: a distilled solution that sacrifices neither utility nor value.

I am wired for pattern recognition, but I distinguish this from templating. Copying other software is just templating. True pattern recognition involves borrowing from the physical world, where interactions feel natural because they are already adopted at scale. I also prioritize removing layers between myself and the user, which is why I moved to Instinct, the veterinary software company, to work directly with the people I serve. I believe designers must think like business owners rather than order-takers, and I avoid getting attached to my work because throwing things away is part of the job. While I appreciate minimal design, I have a soft spot for skeuomorphism and admire the boldness of Apple. Finally, I view AI as an accelerator that amplifies your existing process, making taste the ultimate differentiator in an era where execution is becoming easier for everyone.

chunks.title: Across my notes on processes

TITLE: Across my notes on processes
TAGS: processes, synthesis
TYPE: synthesis | STATUS: settled
CREATED: 2026-05-19 | UPDATED: 2026-07-17
SYNTHESIS across 3 notes

My design process centers on getting as close to the user as possible. I believe every layer between a designer and the person they are solving for acts as a filter that dilutes understanding. This is exactly why I moved to Instinct, the veterinary software company, where I can work directly with veterinarians rather than relying on summaries. I need that direct signal early in a project to ensure my work actually lands.

Before I ever open a design tool, I run through two specific frameworks. First, I define the baseline by identifying what people are doing today. If users are working in a spreadsheet, I have to understand that experience to ensure I never deliver something worse. This baseline is the only way to measure success. Second, I answer six core questions about the problem, the audience, the timing, and the necessity of the work itself. These questions help me navigate the uphill battle of defining a problem clearly. My goal is always to iterate until I reach the simplest version of a solution, because I believe simple is the most elegant form of complexity. I have held these positions since May 2026, and they remain my settled approach for all projects within my Design MOC.
